opus-5.5.text:
I think it's evolved quite a lot, actually, especially in the last couple of years. When I started working on this, maybe five or six years ago, there was very little awareness at all. People thought of AI as something that lived in "the cloud," and the cloud sounded light and fluffy and immaterial. The idea that training a model consumed energy, emitted carbon, used water for cooling data centers, that just wasn't part of the conversation, even among researchers.

Early on, a lot of the work was simply about measurement. We didn't have numbers, so we couldn't have an informed discussion. That's why some colleagues and I built tools like the ML CO2 Impact calculator and contributed to CodeCarbon, so people could estimate the emissions of their own training runs. Then with the BLOOM project at BigScience, we tried to do a full life cycle assessment of a large language model: not just the training, but the manufacturing of the hardware, the idle consumption of the infrastructure, and the deployment.

That deployment piece is where I think understanding has shifted the most. For a long time, the focus was on training, these big one-off numbers that made for nice headlines. But with ChatGPT and the explosion of generative AI being integrated into search, email, everything, people started realizing that inference, using these models millions or billions of times a day, can quickly outweigh the cost of training. And when we compared task-specific models to general-purpose generative models, we found the generative ones can use orders of magnitude more energy for the same task. So using a giant model to do something a small classifier could do is really wasteful.

Now I'd say the public is much more aware. You see news articles about data centers straining power grids, tech companies' emissions going up despite their net-zero pledges, communities pushing back on water usage. That's a big change.

But there's still a big gap, which is transparency. Paradoxically, as awareness has grown, the companies building the biggest models have shared less information. We often don't know model sizes, where they're trained, what hardware, what energy mix. So people are worried, but they lack the numbers to make informed choices, and that's why I've been pushing for things like energy ratings for AI models, a kind of Energy Star for AI, so users and policymakers can actually compare options. Ultimately, I don't want people to feel guilty about using AI; I want them to have the information to use it more mindfully.

r001.rationale: The response says public awareness is now “much more” developed, but does not state that awareness has not become mainstream.

r002.rationale: It describes people viewing AI as living in an immaterial-sounding cloud; it does not say they believe AI runs on users’ phones.

r003.rationale: It says generative models can use orders of magnitude more energy than task-specific models for the same task, but does not compare them with ordinary software.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. It's been a really interesting evolution to watch, honestly. When I started working on this around 2019, 2020, it was very much a niche concern. We'd put out a paper quantifying the carbon footprint of training a model, and the reaction was mostly, "oh, that's neat," and then everyone went back to scaling. It felt like something a handful of us cared about in a corner of the field.

What changed, I think, was ChatGPT. Once these models became something ordinary people used every day, the question shifted from "how much did it cost to train this thing once" to "what does it cost every time I ask it a question." And that's a question people can actually relate to. There was this very viral framing about how a query consumes a bottle of water or whatever, and even though a lot of those numbers were imprecise or taken out of context, they did something important: they made the physical reality of AI visible. Because for most people, AI lives in the cloud. It's this abstraction. And suddenly there's water and electricity and a data center being built down the road from them.

So the awareness is way higher than it was. The downside is that the understanding is still pretty shallow and sometimes wrong in both directions. You get people saying every prompt is destroying the planet, and you get companies saying it's all negligible and we'll solve climate change with AI anyway. Neither is accurate. And the core problem hasn't gone away, which is that we still don't have transparency. The companies deploying these models at scale aren't publishing their energy or water numbers, so we're all doing estimates from the outside. That's why I spend so much time on things like the AI Energy Score, trying to create standardized ways to measure and compare, because you can't have informed public understanding without actual data. Awareness came first. The information to back it up is still catching up.

r001.rationale: The response says awareness is much higher, but does not state that awareness has not become mainstream.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as an abstraction in the cloud; it does not say people believe AI runs on their phones or connect that belief to underestimating impacts.

r003.rationale: The response discusses energy use but does not compare large language models’ energy requirements with ordinary software.

astra-6.text:
I think awareness has grown quite a lot. Initially, the conversation was mostly about the energy required to train these models. People would ask, “What’s the carbon footprint of training a large language model?” That’s an important question, but it’s only one part of the picture.

Now there’s more attention to what happens when you deploy a model and millions of people start interacting with it. There’s also more discussion of water use and the impacts of manufacturing the hardware. So the conversation is expanding beyond just training and beyond just carbon.

But awareness doesn’t necessarily mean we have good information. Companies often aren’t disclosing enough for people to make meaningful comparisons. And the impact depends on things like the model, the task, and where the electricity comes from. It’s difficult to reduce all of that to a single number for an AI query.

What I’d like to see is that growing interest translate into more transparency, so people can understand the tradeoffs and make informed choices.

r001.rationale: The response says awareness has grown, but does not state whether understanding is mainstream.

r002.rationale: It does not mention people believing AI systems run on phones or underestimating their impacts for that reason.

r003.rationale: It discusses energy use but does not compare LLMs’ energy requirements with ordinary software.

sol-6.1.text:
I think awareness has grown a lot. A few years ago, when I talked about the carbon footprint of AI, people were often surprised that there was a footprint at all. AI feels very abstract—you type something into a box and get an answer. You don’t see the data centers, the electricity, or the water needed to cool the hardware.

Now people are asking about those things, which is encouraging. But the conversation still tends to focus on training: how much energy did it take to train this particular model? That’s important, but it’s only part of the picture. Once a model is deployed, potentially millions of people are using it, and each interaction has a cost. You also have to consider manufacturing the hardware.

The challenge is that awareness has moved faster than transparency. People want to know what the impact is, but we often don’t have the information needed to give them a clear answer. It depends on the model, the task, where it’s running, and the energy being used. So I think we’re moving beyond simply recognizing that AI has an environmental impact toward asking how we can measure it and make informed choices.

r001.rationale: It says awareness has grown and more people are asking about impacts, but does not state that awareness remains outside the mainstream.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as abstract and says users do not see data centers, electricity, or cooling water; it does not say people think AI runs on their phones.

r003.rationale: It mentions energy use for training and deployed interactions, but does not compare language models’ energy requirements with ordinary software.
